title: Literals
recap: Every literal has a type. Integer literals are int and floating-point literals are double by default, while suffixes such as u, LL, and f request unsigned int, long long, and float literal types.
A magic value has unclear meaning or may need coordinated changes. Giving domain values names makes calculations understandable and keeps each configurable value in one place.
objectives: Match float, unsigned int, and long long initializers with typed literal suffixes.
Use an uppercase LL suffix and a digit separator for a large integral literal.
Replace literals in a calculation with descriptive named constants.
warnings: An unsuffixed floating-point literal has type double, not float.
Lowercase l can be confused with the digit 1, so uppercase L is preferred.
Do not reintroduce cans-per-case or case-volume magic values in the output expressions.
challenge: Give the three fixed domain values matching const types and typed literals: 1.5f liters per can, 8u cans per case, and 1'000'000LL cans of annual capacity. Compute litersPerCase from the two named per-case values and preserve fixed one-decimal output.
hints: Start by matching each declaration's type to its literal: float uses f, unsigned int uses u, and long long uses LL.
The apostrophe in 1'000'000 is only a visual digit separator; append LL after the final digit.
Define litersPerCase as litersPerCan * cansPerCase so neither 1.5 nor 8 is repeated in the calculation.
